title: Routes, HTTP Methods, and Status Codes
summary: Map methods and paths to handlers, use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE the way clients expect, and answer with the right status code.
intro: Roombook answers one request so far. A real API answers dozens: list the rooms, show one, book it, change the booking, cancel it. Each needs a route, the right HTTP method, and the right status code, and clients rely on all three. A browser retries a GET without asking, a phone app retries a POST on a bad connection, and a client's code checks the status before it reads a word of the body. This lesson builds Roombook's controllers for rooms and bookings with Spring MVC, then goes through the methods one by one, GET and HEAD, POST, PUT and PATCH, and DELETE, and ends with a map of every status code the API sends and when.

steps.title: Routes and path parameters

examples.title: A room that exists
examples.prompt: With `./mvnw spring-boot:run` running, read room 1 from your computer's own terminal.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
examples.explanation: The request matched `GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}`, so Spring called `get` with `roomId` set to the text `"1"`. `Ids.parse` turned it into the number 1, and the repository found room 1, Turing. Jackson turned the `Room` record into JSON, its fields in the order the record declares them: its id, its name, its building's slug, how many people fit, and its amenities. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` means Spring sent the body in pieces, as it wrote it, in place of a `Content-Length` up front. Notice that `id` is the number 1, while `roomId` arrived as text: the one in the body came from Roombook's own data.

examples.title: What a typed parameter does with text
examples.prompt: For comparison, the same route written with `@PathVariable long roomId`, asked for the room `abc`.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 400
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:40 GMT
Connection: close

{"timestamp":"2026-11-21T23:59:40.138Z","status":400,"error":"Bad Request","message":"Method parameter 'roomId': Failed to convert value of type 'java.lang.String' to required type 'long'; For input string: \"abc\"","path":"/v1/rooms/abc"}
examples.explanation: Spring couldn't turn `abc` into a `long`, so it answered 400 before the handler ran, in Spring Boot's own error format, whose `message` names the parameter and the Java types. It also closed the connection, as Tomcat does after many errors. The answer isn't wrong in general, but it isn't Roombook's contract, which says an id that can't exist is simply not found. With `Ids.parse`, the real route answers `{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}` instead, the same as for room 99.

examples.title: A method the path doesn't support
examples.prompt: `-X POST` makes curl send POST instead of GET.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405
Allow: GET, PATCH, PUT, DELETE
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT

{"timestamp":"2026-11-21T23:59:23.850Z","status":405,"error":"Method Not Allowed","message":"Method 'POST' is not supported.","path":"/v1/rooms/1"}
examples.explanation: The path matched, but no POST handler exists for it, so Spring answered 405 by itself. The `Allow` header tells the client's code which methods would have worked, and a developer can read it to see their mistake: to create a room, you POST to `/v1/rooms`. The list's order changes from run to run, and it leaves out HEAD, which works anyway. The body is Spring Boot's own error format, with no `trace` now that `application.yaml` turns it off. The lesson on validation and errors gives Spring's own errors Roombook's format.

steps.title: GET and HEAD: reading

examples.title: Every room
examples.prompt: Without `-i`, curl prints only the body.
examples.explanation: All three rooms come back inside `items`, in id order, since the map keeps its keys sorted. Jackson writes JSON with no spaces or line breaks, the smallest form, which is right for programs and hard for people. To read it comfortably, open the same address in a browser, since Firefox and Chrome both lay JSON out neatly, and the lesson on curl, Postman, and OpenAPI shows jq, the terminal tool most developers use for this.

examples.title: HEAD for the same room
examples.prompt: `-I` sends HEAD and prints the headers it gets back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT
examples.explanation: The status and the `Content-Type` match the GET for room 1, but no body came back. Spring ran the GET handler, which built the whole response, then sent only its head. There's no `Content-Length` either, since this handler's body is written in chunks, and with no chunks there's nothing to count. That's still useful to a client that only needs to know whether room 1 exists: a 200 says yes, and a 404 says no, without paying for the body either way.

steps.title: POST: creating and actions

examples.title: Creating a room
examples.prompt: `--json` sends its text as the body of a POST, and sets `Content-Type: application/json` for you.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: /v1/rooms/4
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT

{"id":4,"name":"Hamilton","building":"science-library","capacity":10,"amenities":["screen"]}
examples.explanation: The repository gave the new room the next id, 4, and the handler answered 201 with `Location: /v1/rooms/4` and the room itself. The single quotes around the JSON keep the terminal from reading its double quotes and brackets as part of the command. `Location` holds a path, not a full URL: the client combines it with the address it called. Run the command again and you get room 5, an identical second room, which is the non-idempotent POST in action.

examples.title: Cancelling a booking
examples.prompt: Booking 1001 is Ada's Algorithms study group in Turing, on Monday 5 October 2026.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT

{"id":1001,"roomId":1,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","attendees":3,"note":"Algorithms study group","status":"cancelled","version":2,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: The action sent no body, since the path says everything: which booking, and what to do. The answer is 200 with the booking, now `"status":"cancelled"` at `"version":2`. The status is a Java enum, `BookingStatus.CANCELLED`, which an annotation tells Jackson to write in lowercase. Run it a second time and the answer is the same 200 and the same body, still version 2, since the handler returns a cancelled booking without cancelling it again.

steps.title: PUT and PATCH: updating

examples.title: Replacing room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 is the Hamilton room the POST created. This PUT sends all four fields, with a new capacity and a new amenity.
examples.explanation: `-X PUT` changes the method `--json` would use, which is POST, and keeps the JSON body and its `Content-Type`. The room now holds exactly what the body said: capacity 12, and both amenities. The id is still 4, because it came from the path, not the body. If the server restarted since the POST, room 4 is gone, since the rooms live in memory, and the answer is the 404: run the POST from the previous part again first.

examples.title: Patching one field
examples.prompt: `-H` sets a header, here the merge patch's own `Content-Type`, and `-d` sends the body.
examples.explanation: Only the capacity changed, to 8. The name, the building, and both amenities stayed as the PUT left them, since the patch didn't mention them, and `requireNonNullElse` kept each current value. `-d` alone would send `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, the type an HTML form uses, and Spring would refuse it, as the next lesson shows. Setting the header with `-H` tells Roombook it's a merge patch.

examples.title: A PUT that leaves fields out
examples.prompt: The same room, replaced with a body that has only a name.
examples.explanation: The room lost its building, its capacity, and its amenities, now all `null`. The handler did what PUT promises and stored exactly what it got, and Jackson set every missing field of the `RoomInput` to `null`. This is the classic PUT mistake: a client meant to rename the room and sent only the name. The fix is on both sides. Clients use PATCH to change some fields, and the API rejects a PUT that's missing required fields, which the lesson on validation and errors adds with a 422 that names each missing one.

steps.title: DELETE and what each method promises
steps.body:
Deleting is the change you can't take back, and it's also one that clients retry a lot, since a delete that timed out leaves them unsure whether it happened. So it needs an answer that's clear the first time and safe the second.

## 204 No Content

`DELETE /v1/rooms/{roomId}` removes the room and answers **204 No Content**: it worked, and there's nothing to send back.

```java
@DeleteMapping("/{roomId}")
public ResponseEntity<Object> delete(@PathVariable String roomId) {
    Optional<Room> room = find(roomId);
    if (room.isEmpty()) {
        return notFound();
    }
    rooms.remove(room.get().id());
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
```

`noContent().build()` sends the 204 with no body.

## Soft delete

In memory, Roombook simply removes the room. With a database, it won't. Bookings point at their room, and a booking from last month must still be able to say it was in Turing, so erasing the room would break its history. Instead, Roombook does a **soft delete**: it keeps the room and marks it inactive, and every read skips inactive rooms. To clients, it's gone. To the records, it's still there. The lesson on raw SQL adds the `active` column that does this.

Deleting has a rule too: a room with upcoming bookings can't be deleted, because the students who booked it would show up to a room that no longer exists in the system. That gets **409 Conflict**, the code for a request that clashes with the current state of the data.

## The second DELETE

After the first DELETE, the room is gone. What should a second, identical DELETE answer? There are two sound choices:

- **204 again**: the client wanted the room gone, and it is.
- **404**: there's no room there to delete.

Either keeps DELETE idempotent, because idempotent means the server ends up in the same state, not that the answer is the same. Roombook answers 404, since nothing is there, and its clients treat a 404 from a DELETE as done. What matters is choosing one and answering it every time, so client developers can rely on it.

## What each method promises

Here's every method Roombook uses, and the promises clients build on:

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Request body | Cacheable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | yes | yes | no | yes |
| HEAD | yes | yes | no | yes |
| POST | no | no | yes | rarely |
| PUT | no | yes | yes | no |
| PATCH | no | no | yes | no |
| DELETE | no | yes | no | no |
| OPTIONS | yes | yes | no | no |

- **Safe** methods change nothing, so anything may send them at any time.
- **Idempotent** methods can be retried after a timeout without doing the work twice. A client library may retry GET, PUT, and DELETE by itself, but never POST.
- **Request body** says whether the method carries one. A GET or DELETE with a body is allowed by the rules but has no agreed meaning, and many proxies and libraries drop it, so never design an API that needs one.
- **Cacheable** responses may be stored and reused by browsers and caches, which is how a second visit gets faster. A POST answer can only be reused in rare cases most caches ignore.

## OPTIONS

**OPTIONS** asks a server which methods a path supports, and the answer's `Allow` header lists them. Spring answers it for every route by itself, as the third example shows. Browsers send OPTIONS on their own before some requests from other origins, the CORS preflight from the web course. The security lesson sets up the answers those need.

examples.title: Deleting room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 must exist, so run the POST that creates it first if the server restarted.
examples.explanation: The answer is only a status line and a `Date` header: no `Content-Type`, no `Content-Length`, and no body, since a 204 has none. Everything a client needs is in the status: the room is deleted. `GET /v1/rooms` no longer lists it, and its id isn't reused, since the repository's counter only goes up. Reusing ids would let an old link to room 4 point at a different room.

examples.title: Deleting it again
examples.prompt: The same command, run a second time.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT

{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}
examples.explanation: `find` found no room 4, so the handler answered 404 before it reached the delete. The server's state is the same as after the first DELETE, which is what makes the method idempotent, even though the status differs. A client that sent the first DELETE, lost the answer, and retried, sees this 404 and knows its goal is met: the room is gone either way.

examples.title: Asking which methods work
examples.prompt: `-X OPTIONS` sends an OPTIONS request for room 1.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Allow: GET,HEAD,PATCH,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS
Accept-Patch:
Accept-Query:
Content-Length: 0
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:59:23 GMT
examples.explanation: Spring built the `Allow` list from the controller's annotations: the four methods it declares for `/{roomId}`, plus HEAD and OPTIONS, which it answers for every route. Unlike the 405 answer in the first part, this list includes HEAD. The two empty headers come from Spring too: `Accept-Patch` would list the body types a PATCH accepts, and `Accept-Query` those of a newer method, QUERY, and Spring leaves them blank here. Nothing to maintain: add a method to the controller, and it appears in the list.

steps.title: Status codes: the full map
steps.body:
The status code is the first thing a client's code reads, before a single byte of the body. It decides what happens next: show the data, show an error, retry, send the user to log in, or give up. An API that picks its codes carefully lets every client handle every answer correctly without parsing error messages.

## The questions, in order

When a request comes in, an API answers a series of questions, and the first one that fails picks the code. Each later lesson builds one of these checks, but the order already tells you which code to send:

```diagram routes-and-methods-status-codes
Each no leads to its code, and the first one that applies wins.
```

## Every code Roombook sends

| Code | Roombook sends it when |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | a read, an update, or an action worked |
| 201 Created | a POST made a room or a booking |
| 202 Accepted | work was queued, to finish later |
| 204 No Content | a DELETE worked |
| 304 Not Modified | the client's saved copy is still current |
| 400 Bad Request | the request can't be read, like broken JSON |
| 401 Unauthorized | there's no valid login, token, or key |
| 403 Forbidden | the caller is known, but not allowed |
| 404 Not Found | no route matches, or no such room or booking |
| 405 Method Not Allowed | the path exists, but not with that method |
| 409 Conflict | the room is already booked at that time |
| 412 Precondition Failed | an `If-Match` header names an old version |
| 413 Content Too Large | the body is over the size limit |
| 415 Unsupported Media Type | the body isn't JSON |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | the JSON is fine, but a value breaks a rule |
| 429 Too Many Requests | the caller is over its rate limit |
| 500 Internal Server Error | a bug, or a crash |
| 502 Bad Gateway | a service Roombook called gave a broken answer |
| 503 Service Unavailable | Roombook is overloaded, or shutting down |
| 504 Gateway Timeout | a service Roombook called didn't answer in time |

In Java, Spring's `HttpStatus` enum names each one, like `HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND` and `HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT`. Tomcat sends only the number on the status line, and Spring Boot's error answers give the name in their `error` field.

## Pairs that people mix up

- **401 or 403.** 401 means we don't know who you are: log in, or send a valid token. 403 means we know exactly who you are, and you still can't do this, like a member creating a room, which only staff may do.
- **400 or 422.** 400 means the request can't be read at all, like JSON with a missing bracket. 422 means it was read fine, and a value breaks a rule, like booking a room for 6 with 40 attendees.
- **409 or 412.** 409 means the request clashes with the data as it is, like booking a slot that's taken. 412 means the client made its request conditional on a version, with `If-Match`, and the data has changed since it looked, so the server refused to apply a change based on an old copy.

## 4xx or 5xx: who must act

A **4xx** means the client must change something. Sending the same request again gets the same answer, so a client shouldn't retry it as it is. Two are exceptions worth knowing: after a 429, a client waits as long as the `Retry-After` header says and tries again, and after a 409, it can read the latest data and then decide.

A **5xx** means the server failed, and the request itself may have been fine. A retry a little later may work, especially after a 502, 503, or 504. But only retry what's safe to repeat: a GET, a PUT, a DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key, from the reliability lesson. Retrying a plain POST after a 504 can book a room twice, since the first request may have worked before the answer was lost.

## Never 200 for an error

Some APIs answer every request with 200, and put `{"error": "..."}` in the body. Don't. Caches store a 200 and hand the error to the next person, monitoring counts it as a success, and every client has to read the body to find out that something went wrong. In Spring, a handler that returns a value sends 200, and `ResponseEntity.status(...)` picks any other code, which is what `ApiError.response` does. Roombook's own errors are a first draft for now, Spring's 400s and 405s are in Spring Boot's format, and the lesson on validation and errors gives all of them one shape.

The next lesson reads everything else a request carries: the query string, the headers, and the body.

recap:
- A route is a method plus a path pattern, like GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}, and Spring picks the most specific match.
- `@PathVariable String` plus Ids.parse turns an id that isn't valid into a 404, where a typed long would give 400.
- Spring answers 404, 405 with an Allow header, HEAD, and OPTIONS by itself, in Spring Boot's error format.
- GET and HEAD only read, so crawlers, caches, and retries can send them at any time.
- POST creates with ResponseEntity.created, a 201, and a Location header, runs actions like cancel, and isn't safe to repeat.
- PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent, and PATCH with JSON Merge Patch changes only the fields it sends.
- DELETE answers 204 with noContent, Roombook soft-deletes rooms, and a second DELETE gets 404 every time.
- 4xx means the client must change the request, 5xx means the server failed, and an error never gets 200.
